5.quote: Refrain from expressing past hardships upon achieving success; with time, they will become apparent.

6.quote: The only way to gain a stranger's trust is to be good at their game.

7.quote: When you can't make a choice, flip a coin and let fate decide.

8.quote: Fire can be used both to light up and to burn down the world; so can a human being.

9.quote: Examine from others. Execute for others. Educate others.

10.quote: Stay innocent. When your heart and mind are pure, you see things that others can't, you get help that others won't, and you show love that others don't.

11.quote: It is only when you have done all you can and are still lost that you should turn to him.
11.story:
My college ended and I came home with empty hands. My parents were supportive and I had good faith too in what I did during those days. So I started applying for jobs. 20 days went by and I did not get any offer. Then one of my school friends messaged me saying all of them are gathering for a birthday celebration. It's been more than 6 years, so I too wanted to visit at first, but I still didn't get my job and If I tell my parents I am going out with friends, their first thought would be "How come he is so unserious about his career? Is this the time to all these things?" If I ignore them and visit my friends, for the rest of the time I'm jobless, they won't treat me properly. If I stay at my house, my friends will think "It's been 6 years, all of the gang is coming, why not him?" My friends knew I rarely hang out with them. Our only relationship was at school, and rarely beyond that. I had two choices, and me choosing one will definitely affect the other. I realized that either way, damage was going to happen.

Then I went into an empty room, took the "thing"(don't want to mention) of him, closed my eyes and thought. "You are seeing this. You tell me, what am I supposed to do? I put good effort into both of them, now can't I have both?" Then I just continued with my job applications. After half an hour, I got a selection email and a small assignment. It was the first in two years since I began my preparing. I told my parents, and they were happy. I also told them there was enough time to finish the assignment, and that my friends were calling me. They didn't mind as I have some control over my schedule. Then I visited my friends, and everything went well. While I was returning home, on an empty, dark road, I saw the exact thing I had that reminded me of him. In that moment, I felt him with me, and I knew for sure that I was not alone on that road.

12.quote:
Compassion toward your enemies is a sign of a pure heart, for you are not blinded by their hatred.
Confrontation with your friends is a sign of a pure mind, for you are not blinded by their love.

13.quote: Belief makes you plant the seed. Intention brings you its fruits.

14.quote: If you do something with love and care, it feels like a hobby to you, while it looks like hard work to others.
14.story:
During school, my father enrolled me in maths tuition because the board exams were coming and I was just average at maths. Initially I didn't like going to that tuition, but it had an air conditioner. This alone made me go to tuition directly from school, stay there until night, and then return home. In the first few days, I just did my homework by searching for answers in guides. Gradually, though, I started noticing new formulae and techniques that I didn't know yet. It felt fascinating; most of the problems could be solved in six or seven steps. This got me interested in maths. It helped me perform well in my board exams, then in the next school, and also helped me get good marks in JEE Mains. I got into college, but during the first two years, because of the Covid lockdown, I didn't do anything academically. It was only at the end of my fourth semester, due to a chain of events, that I chose ML as my hobby. Since I was good at maths, I understood most of the concepts easily, and this made me passionate about ML.

I always used to write down new things about new topics on A4 sheets. I bought a 500-page set (thrice), kept it in my room, and used it daily. Similarly, I started writing notes for other subjects, like programming languages and core CS subjects. Fast forward to the end of my fourth year: I had written around 1,500 pages of handwritten notes (pages, not papers, not to be mistaken). My friend saw this and was shocked. He couldn't believe I still wasn't placed at a good company, and he said, "Your hard work will definitely pay off. Don't worry." Little did he know, there was no hard work in that process. Never once did I feel pain in my hands or exhaustion while writing them. I simply liked ML and wanted to go as deep as I could. I decided to spiral-bind the ML notes (around 900 pages), but the shopkeeper told me it was too much work to finish. So I did it myself, and it took me six straight hours. I must confess, that was exhausting. I started at 11 and finished at 5. I occasionally read them, because since ChatGPT came along, I mostly turn to it for answers. Eventually I got a job, and now I am doing well. But those pages are lying inside my suitcase, waiting for me to look back on them someday in the far future.

15.quote: Only three things can cause a transformation: fear of the future, love in the present, and pain from the past. In rare cases, a revelation.

16.quote: On a long journey, worry more about losing your comfort than about reaching your destination.

17.quote: The strong have the courage to apologize. The mighty have the wisdom to foresee such situations and avoid them.
17.story:
I saw an image on social media that said something like, "Share your hot takes, and we won't judge." I got curious and went through the comments. The top comment said something like, "I'll never share it, no matter what, because no one would understand." People in the replies were begging the person to reveal it, while others were blaming him for making them even more curious.

After scrolling somewhat deep into the comments, I finally found his explanation, and it was absolutely horrifying. Everyone under that comment were speechless. He did apologize, but once words leave your mouth, you are no longer in control of them... There I understood why it had become the top comment. The next day, that image appeared on my feed again with even more likes, but that top comment was nowhere to be found.

18.quote: When offered in abundance, take limited or decline entirely.

19.quote: Pain by fate is an experience. Pain by choice is a conviction. One happens to you; the other reveals you.

20.quote: Keep them in. Let them die inside; they will spring up beautifully sometime later. Otherwise, if you let them out, they will only serve to bury you.

21.quote: Love is born only after destiny is fulfilled. When destiny is complete, the good and bad in you die, leaving behind nothing but innocence, and from that innocence, love is born.
21.story:
Looking back, during my JEE preparation I didn't really have a goal. I was simply attending classes and taking tests because that's what the people around me did. I knew this mattered for admission to a prestigious university, but I wasn't really aware of how big a deal it was. Despite that, I still loved my subjects. I was good at math, average at physics, and quite bad at chemistry. That was also the period when my migraine was at its worst, and I hadn't yet figured out how to control or stop it. Because of this invisible suffering, I treated people with hostility. I used to hate smiling, and I hated people who smiled or laughed. The pain was excruciating, lasting 8-9 months a year, 15-20 days a month, and 8-10 hours a day. I don't know the cause, and I still can't find it to this day, but I suspect my nerves aren't getting enough nutrition from the food I eat. I believe my gut isn't absorbing nutrients properly. This affected my life significantly. I was not kind to my parents, and I avoided spending much time with my friends. I had a tablet and spent a lot of time on it. I knew the ultimate goal at that time was to get into a good university, but my body was becoming a hurdle. Then the results came, and they were devastating. I used to cycle at least 25 km, travelling from home to school and then to tuition, at the age of 16-17. I knew that even if I wasn't good at my studies, this hard work would pay off. It didn't. Then I chose a college with a very low tuition fee, and I got in. Classes were online because of Covid. I hated my classmates; they all came from various backgrounds. Also, in a college like this, you won't find many people who are serious about their careers. I was only in touch with one guy from my class throughout the first two years. Online classes never felt serious, and some teachers taught in Hindi, which I didn't understand. So I just kept the window open and played games. Then one day they announced that college was reopening. I had been waiting for this moment all four years. I still had migraines, and I was very scared of how I was going to stay alone in a completely new environment. Then I reached Bilaspur, found a PG, and settled in.

Two years later, that was the best my life had ever been, and it still is. For the first time in 18 or 19 years, I interacted with people on my own, and they turned out to be kind, helpful, and loving. The people in my PG, my teachers, my classmates, my neighbours, everyone. Also, my class had its own groups. There were several friendship circles, each with their own little world. Although the groups weren't really close to one another, they were all close to me. My father once said behind my back that my life was supposed to be a punishment for my negligence of academics and for how I treated the people around me. He said that after I was done with it, there would be a transformation. He was right, except that for the people who knew me, it looked like a punishment. But not for me. During that life, I became a completely new person. A person who always showed love and cared for others. For example, I had near 100% attendance because I wanted to see my friends everyday, Sun or rain, I used to show up to class. I always ate my food at mess without wasting any, because I loved the people at my mess. Whenever my friends asked for help with their projects, I used to go to their rooms and complete it. All the bad thoughts I used to have about people behind their backs were gone. Everything I thought I knew about life fell apart. In those two years, I learned good morals again from scratch. It was like going back to kindergarten to learn the basics. I was valued at my job, and loved by my family, my relatives, my friends, and everyone who came to know me from that point. I have received so many compliments from friends and strangers. The pain is still there, but life rewarded me with techniques to control it. The people I once hated became the people who I care about deeply. Was this simply due to changing the environment? Every environment has its own good and bad sides. So was mine, My hostel was the WORST in that entire area, many of my friends acknowledged it. Cows, snakes, dogs used to enter in. Many people who cam to my mess also told that the food was bad. I still lived there, because love gave me the power to endure them. It is what I saw and took in that cause this change. This is my destiny. From a person who refused to show love to becoming the very person who lives with it. From that moment on, I never once thought of harming them or anyone new I might meet hereafter, because who knows? I might end up loving them too. This is how a child treats the world. I thought I had failed JEE and ended up in a cheap college, but would succeeding there have brought about this transformation? What else can I consider as destiny besides this? The migraine and my poor performance was indirectly leading me to this path. Everything about my old self simply died, and I am no longer that person. I'm finally in love with my life, something my old self never was, yet something a part of it had always longed to be.

22.quote: Your trust in my beliefs should not be based solely on my position in life, but rather on your own instincts. Your decisions reveal a lot about your position in life.

23.quote: Redemption comes only when you let something inside you go.

24.quote: Focusing on different layers of a music piece can make you feel like you are listening to different music pieces.

25.quote: In a vast universe, nothing may seem miraculous; in a small one, everything may seem miraculous.
25.story:
When I was a child, I had a habit of waking up in the middle of the night, drinking a stomach full of cold water, and going back to sleep. One time, I was trying to get water from the fridge. I opened the door, took the water, and drank as much as I could. When I tried to close it, I noticed something different. I hadn't completely closed the fridge, yet I felt the room get darker quite early. I opened it again, and another realization struck me. The light turned on a split second after I opened the door, and the same thing happened when I closed it. It felt like magic. I intentionally closed the fridge door as slowly as I could, and I did see the exact moment the light changed. For many days I wondered how that was even possible. Was it magic? I thought the light had to stay on all the time inside the fridge, and that it only went dark when the power went off.

It has been many years since then. Now I know why the lights went off. At the hinge, there was a button and a pad. As I close the fridge, the pad moves toward that button, presses it, and holds it. Because of that, the light goes off. When I open the door, the pad moves away, releasing the button, and the light comes back. At that time, my "world" was quite small. It consisted of my parents, friends, toys, TV shows, and school books. Anything that didn't belong to those simply felt fascinating. Now I know the light was never magic. But I haven't yet found anything that makes me feel that way again.

27.quote: Either cover your eyes, or make sure the light doesn't reflect off your iris.

29.quote: The cruelest thing about being a human, is having a heart capable of producing endless love, yet a mind that can only bear so much of it.
29.story:
My office ends at 8 PM, and it takes up to 10 or 10:30 PM for me to reach home. Honestly, most of the time I won't be exhausted. But on some days, it's a different story. I have to confess something. My mother is not really an expert at cooking all the dishes equally well. Some are really good, and some are just plain bad. Most of the time, I knew the consequences of complaining about a dish. There was once when I asked beforehand, "What's the food tonight?" while I was travelling back to home.  She told me it was a special tomato curry with tortillas. I was really excited. When I came home and saw it, it was the regular bland tomato curry with just some curry leaves and pepper. All my excitement vanished. It also tasted too tangy, so I couldn't eat much of it. I was thinking about what would happen if I said it was bad. So I just kept eating. I held myself together well enough.

When I finished and took my plate to throw away the excess, she saw and said, "You could have eaten more. It tastes really good." That was it for me. I was still aware of what could go wrong, so I politely told her, "You could have brought some chips for 10 rupees and used the curd we have. This simple combination is far tastier than the hours spent making and cooking this food." She smiled and said, "Yeah, we just didn't have enough rice, and we're trying to make it last until the end of the month." Then she said, "You don't like tortillas, right? Next time I'll make rice separately for you." That's when I felt really bad, although I won't say the mistake was mine. After several minutes, she came into my room and brought me bananas. After several more minutes, she came back with a sweet she had made a few days earlier and kept in the fridge. A few minutes later, she came back again and asked what I wanted to eat tomorrow.

That's when I realized I could have just adjusted. I had the right to complain, but I blamed a person who had good intentions. My heart was reminding me there would be consequences, but my mind just ran out of patience.

30.quote: Something magical definitely happened in the past. Different people saw it in different ways, giving birth to different beliefs.
30.story:
I was watching a YouTube video titled something like "Religions Explained." After it ended, I saw another similar video, called something like "Mythologies Explained." I watched both, and they left me amused. There were many things in common across the stories. They had gods who were connected with elements of nature and life, similar animals, similar struggles, and similar events. "How could they all be this close?" I wondered. It definitely didn't seem like made-up fiction, but when considered in an actual sense, they seem quite impossible. I suspect the original meaning or metaphor was lost as the texts were derived and refined.

It's fascinating to realize that all of us share the same roots. Sometimes I even wonder how a content creator who is not even remotely connected to me knows the things that happened in my life when they make videos like "All your pain in one video." It turns out that others just like me, who are also far from one another, feel the same way. What is the one hidden thing that relates all of us? Is it the transfer of knowledge across generations and time, even the trivial parts? The same event can happen to different people and lead each of them to interpret it differently. They often argue that theirs is the truth, but they forget to acknowledge that the magic did happen in the past.

31.quote: Save what is near. Trust what is lost to find its way back.

32.quote: Water must be offered to the pump first, only then do we get more of it.
32.story:
I learnt one of the most valuable lessons from someone I least expected. When I first met him in college, he seemed like a regular person. He dressed fashionably, had dyed his hair, and wore torn jeans. My first thought was, "He isn't very mature." After some time, the five of us, including him, were walking back to our rooms after class. It was 1:30 PM, and the walk usually takes half an hour. We stopped near a shop to buy juice. We sat, talked and had our juice. I was taking my 20 rupees out of my pocket, then I saw him go to the GPay scanner and pay 100 rupees. My first question was why he had paid for all of us. I didn't ask him straight away, but I thought about it for quite a while, until another time when we were in a similar situation. This time, another guy and he argued over who would pay. I wondered whether these people were rich.

Time passed, and we became friends because we used to sit on the same bench and lived in nearby hostels. I saw him asking many of his friends for money. I also saw him giving money to many of them. Most of the amounts were small, but he still had the heart to help a stranger like me and many others. He asked me for money too, because I was the only person in the entire college who didn't have a UPI account. So whenever he needs cash, I am the first person he turns to. He always paid me back, though, and I was amazed by his generosity. Fast forward, college ended and I got a job. Along the way, I too learned a lot and grew as a person. One random day, he messaged me. He was in serious trouble and needed a large amount of money. It was a significant portion of my monthly salary, but I didn't hesitate. I wanted to repay him for all the good he had done over the years by helping others. He had given away pennies to so many people, and when he needed help the most, a substantial sum came his way through me. I sent the money, and it's been over a year now, but I still haven't received it back. We are still in touch, and he often tells me that he will definitely return it one day. I'm not in any hurry. I don't have any health or financial issues, so I'm okay with how things are.

The money is still unpaid, and I am still waiting. But some debts are measured in money, while others are measured in trust. I knew him well enough to believe that I will get it back someday.

33.quote: Failing to recognize the struggles of those around you will only leave you with a struggle that is even harder for others to recognize.

34.quote: A crisis of enthusiasm doesn't warrant a lifetime of suffering.
34.story:
I went to a doctor to get my eyes checked. I already had -2.0 vision in both eyes. I was really nervous because every time I visit the doctor, my prescription increases quite a bit. He checked my eyes and later told me that my prescription had increased by 0.5. I panicked and asked him, "Will the change never stop?" He replied, "As time passes, your body grows older and becomes weaker." I panicked even more and told him, "Now it's 2.5, then after two years, it'll be 4.5, and after ten years, it'll be 14.5, then 40, 50, etc.?" He said, "Shut up and don't argue with me." He was angry because I panicked and shouted while asking that question. Had he told me that the vision stabilizes after a certain point, I would have happily slept that night.

It's been four years. My eyesight is now -3.5, and I've stopped worrying about it. I thought I would have a rough life because my eyesight is directly connected to my migraines. Just thirty seconds without my spectacles can cause an extremely painful headache. I've learned ways to adapt to that, mostly by living a life bounded by limitations, very limited activities, to be precise. Somehow, what I thought would become a lifelong source of suffering hasn't even remained something to fear after all this time.

49.quote: If you see the struggle, you won't feel jealous.
49.story:
In college, my friend had a friend from another state. Neither of them knew the other's language, so they talked in English. He used to walk with us when we went to and from college. I wondered why he stuck with him when people from his own state were also in our college. Some months passed, and we also talked occasionally, but not that closely. As far as I knew, he used to skip classes often. Then I came to know from another friend that he was preparing for GATE. I was also planning to take that exam, but I wasn't really serious about it. My mutual friend told me he scored well in GATE mock tests. One day I went to one of my friends' rooms. As it happened, he was in the next room. I saw him through the window, studying. I watched him for at least three straight minutes, and he seemed really focused on his GATE preparation. His roommate, who was walking by outside, saw me and quietly whispered, "He goes to lunch, comes back at 11 AM, and doesn't move from his place until 8 PM for dinner." What I heard and saw at that same moment filled me with a deep sense of empathy. I thought to myself, "I hope he gets good results. I don't want his effort to go to waste."

Then the exam was over, and the results came out. He got a top 1% score, and I got around the top 10%. I was equally happy about my own result, since I had only written the exam to put the score on my resume, not for higher studies. He, on the other hand, got into one of the country's most prestigious universities. That was the first time I truly felt happy for someone else's achievement. Because usually, when someone announces their success, I was always skeptic and just didn't have the heart to accept that someone is better than me. But the moment when I saw the struggle, I was on his side. Now when I see an achievement, I try to picture the hours they put in that everybody missed to see.

50.quote: The memory of you is a visitor to the temple of the mind. Whomever you enter, leave it a better place.

51.quote: Effort does not take time. Results take time. Ironically, effort itself is a result.
51.story:
Years ago, I think vaguely around 2017, there was a test. I was among the only four students who passed it out of 36 students in the class. I asked my friends who had passed, "Did you go to tuition?" One said, "I analyzed previous years' questions, found patterns, and used them in my preparation." Another said, "I just covered the whole syllabus during the preparation holidays, so I was ready for this." Another said, "I didn't actually study, I looked at the grading system and mark distribution first. I mastered the high weightage, easy to score sections just enough to pass." Whereas I, the fourth guy, had already been in that field for quite a long time, so regardless of the test, I was already aware of most of the things that were asked.

I thought, we four used four different ways to get to the one top, but what about the others? I don't think they wouldn't have prepared... more or less, they would have used similar strategies... so it just wasn't meant to be for them? There is no chance I'm going to insult them with a cheap cliché like 'everything happens for a reason.' One might have missed a pattern that others saw, one might have prepared the kind of questions that were completely exempted this time, one might have crammed the entire syllabus and yet been faced with questions that tested analytical thinking... one might have prepared well with a mentor's guidance, yet on exam day he might have gotten sick... so they all are considered as failure? In a short period of time, with limited opportunities, even taking shortcuts and simply getting lucky could put you on par with people who have put in the effort. But in a lifetime, luck will eventually run out and gimmicks just don't work. In an exam there is high variance... some get lucky, others don't.. but as life goes on, everyone gets their share of luck so it becomes a neutral playing field. Those who put in the effort for that exam won't really have to do anything differently to show up here, too... but those who failed, despite their efforts, need to realize that throughout the process, they have gained new knowledge, developed new ways of thinking, learned how to approach and tackle problems, and built competence... all of which are qualities that winners already possess and that both can draw upon in the next test they face.

52.quote: Never show your anger towards a mob, for a single drop cannot drown you, but an ocean can.
52.story:
At my JEE coaching institute, my batch was the last one and the most ignored, since all the top rankers were in the other batch. I didn't care at the time. Years later, I was going through old emails and saw messages from "myPAT," a platform developed by them. This made me nostalgic, and I wanted to revisit my tuition days. While searching for news about the institute, I found that it had permanently closed. I got curious and searched to find out what had happened. I ended up at a video of the CEO shouting at his employees. He said he had been unwell for the past few days, and I understood that he was not in a good emotional state to address his staff, yet he did so anyway. The anger he showed toward his employees made the video popular. That incident drew a lot of attention, and eventually the institute was shut down.

The most plausible explanation I could find for the collapse is poor planning. The people under him were not shown any care; they were denied salaries for up to four months. The way he behaved toward his own people in that video was paving the way for his downfall. People are assets. I understand there were a lot of debts, but if he had really cared for his people, he should have taken loans, merged institutes, moved all classes online to significantly reduce rent and other property-related expenses, and redirected those savings towards paying staff salaries. But did he? It's easy for me to say while I am comfortably inside four walls observing the situation. But I acknowledge that the reality is very different. Still, I am very sure that his disregard for his people was the problem after all.

53.quote: Many events in life follow an exponential or logarithmic pattern. Know where you stand, in time and space.

54.quote: A bag contains 1,000 red balls and 1 blue ball. You close your eyes and pick one. Luck is when you get a blue ball. A miracle is when you get a green ball.
54.story:
After my JEE was over, I was left with a fairly disappointing score card. At that time, I did not know that I could apply to my local colleges with my board exam marks. I only found out after the deadline ended, which left my JEE percentile as my only hope. JoSAA had six rounds, and at each round the leftover seats were carried over to the next one. I applied to colleges that accept fairly low scores. When round one ended, I did not get a college. My parents and I had no reaction at all. When round two ended, it was the same result. There was slight hope that something would turn out well in the next four rounds. When round three ended, I still had no college, and the fear grew. If I did not get a seat within the six rounds, I would have to join a private college where the fees are stupidly high. We could not spend that much money, since we had already poured everything we had into my JEE coaching fees. When round four ended, I still had nothing, and the fear kept building. For context, there are three to four days between each round, so the longer the rounds went on, the more fear came. When round five ended, my family was panicking, and there was gloom in our house. If I did not get a college in the next one, I would have to wait a whole year for the next admission process and take the exam again, which, given the situation, was devastating. Round six ended, and I still had no college, which was enough to break me. I was silent for a long time because I was hiding the news from my parents. I knew I had lost. I was unreactive for at least two or three hours. All hope was gone. I was desperate for a miracle and ready to pay whatever it took. I kept repeating his in my head for help.

Some time passed, I ate lunch, and my parents began to suspect something. Then, to my surprise, I saw a video titled "All you need to know about CSAB" with a college thumbnail. I clicked it, and there was my second chance. Apparently, the vacant seats after the admission rounds are set up to be filled again. I learned there were two rounds for this. I told my parents the news, but they still had no hope for me. I believed this was the miracle I needed. "Accidentally," I came across a college with a much lower tuition fee than many colleges in India. I applied, and in the first round I got a seat. My parents looked into the college and told me it was a decent college and that I had to make good use of it. It turns out CSAB was always meant to happen after JoSAA. I just didn't know that. For others, it was no surprise, but for me, it was a revelation when I was in dire need. A miracle isn't an event with zero probability. It's an event that looks impossible because of what we know, while the reality was always different. This is why the same event can feel obvious to one person and shocking to another. As I know nothing of what lies ahead, and so little of what simply is, I am certain life will always find ways to amuse me.

55.quote: Neither of us was any different; had I been born in his place, I, too, would have turned out just like him. He was only a child, as I was.

56.quote: Just one 'I' to be; a universe of effort lies beneath.
56.story:
I was returning to Chennai from Bilaspur. The train runs only once a week. The journey is roughly around 25-26 hours. So I had to pack food for afternoon and night, but I decided to buy food from the train. Now I went to the railway station at least an hour before... I saw my train, and the workers were cleaning the seats. I was outside. There was a booth that offered drinking water. I filled my water bottle. Then a person came to me selling pillows and blankets. I didn't needed it at that time. Then another person came to me selling snacks, I denied again. Then another person came to me to prepare food. I brought food from him. Then a person next to my seat used the socket nearby to charge his phone. I saw a pattern there... Everything we needed was ready for us. Of course they are doing their job, trying to make profits, but for me it was like a service.

The train driver stays awake all night, carefully driving the train. The chefs inside cook food for the travellers. The sellers show us all kinds of things we would need on a journey. A large number of people work behind the screens at the railways, coordinating all the services. Even outside the train journey, cab drivers are ready to take me home, and police and security keep everyone safe. For me to complete a journey, a huge number of people must work and make things happen. This is just a small glimpse of life. Imagine any scenario; it is most likely to be like this. Now imagine this happening throughout the world. Now imagine it happening for years... even from the beginning of time itself. You exist because they happened to be.

57.quote: You have reached the top of the mountain. Congratulations. Now, you must come down, as staying there is not safe.
57.story:
I changed to a new school after my grade 10 was over. There I remained mostly quiet and kept to myself. I was not involved in any trouble, and I was a good student in class. Even my teacher once told the whole class, "Swami Vivekananda himself has come to Vivekananda Senior Secondary School." I was not really that good at academics, yet I managed to get first rank in my class, thanks to the JEE coaching. When I moved into class 12, I became known to other classes, and even in my own class, friends started talking to me more. That success boosted my confidence. I started talking with my friends a lot, even ignoring classes by spending time playing with a Rubik's cube under the desk and playing games on our notebooks. I boasted about my success and said I just didn't belong there among those people. I argued with my teachers on purpose to create a funny incident so my friends would laugh. I never did any experiment in the chemistry lab sincerely. My teachers knew I had been preparing for JEE since grade 11, but they had never seen me behave so shabbily before. Then the quarterly exams came, and I failed physics. That was the first time I had failed a subject for as long as I could remember. The red ink in my report card humbled me. My teacher asked my father, "What's this, sir? 'JEE' coaching? What happened?" It was not his fault, yet he was embarrassed. He didn't really blame me, but he told me, "I think this should be enough for you to realize."

Was that really my fault? It was the first time in my life that I had ever won at anything. I was good at math in my previous school, but my skills didn't really make me stand out or bring me fame. I just didn't know how to handle the victory. Looking back, it was nature's way of putting me on the right path. Thankfully, it happened in school itself; otherwise, if it had happened later in my life, it would have been irredeemable. Fast-forward to the final examination, where I got the highest marks in physics along with some other students, but did it matter? The damage was done. Deep down, I always felt that I owed my teachers an apology.

58.quote: We often mistakenly make an unfair comparison between the sadness of the present and the happiness of the past.

59.quote: When your mind cannot find an answer but your heart longs for one, step into a new reality. The heart will show the mind the way.
59.story:
In Kung Fu Panda (2008), Po did not accept Shifu as his master because he simply didn't believe that Shifu could train him within such a limited period of time. Shifu knew this too. After the argument they had that night, Shifu was left alone at the peach tree, where all the leaves had fallen along with Oogway the previous night, desperately looking for a clue on how to train Po. He heard Po's movements and the noises he made while searching for food. Watching him, Shifu wondered, "What is this guy even doing?" He then hinted that the cookies were on the top shelf, which excited Po and motivated him to find a way to reach them. Shifu was amused by Po's desire for food and by how he was able to push beyond his limitations just to get something to eat. That was the moment it clicked for Shifu. He took Po to the Sacred Pool of Tears, where he declared that Po was going to learn kung fu and that he, Shifu, was his master. Po finally accepted him.

Po always wanted to learn kung fu with all his heart, but his mind kept reminding him of reality: Shifu might not be able to turn him into the dragon warrior, even if he had a hundred years before Tai Lung arrived. But something changed when he stepped into the Pool of Sacred Tears. Standing in a place where Oogway himself had unravelled the mysteries of harmony and focus, Po seemed to experience something beyond ordinary excitement. Perhaps, for the first time, his dream didn't feel so distant anymore. The place and its significance, with Shifu's decision to bring him there made something click inside him. It was as though the bell finally rang within Po, convincing his mind to trust what his heart had always wanted. There, in that sacred place, both student and master were finally ready to begin. And the rest was history.

60.quote: There is life in every non-living thing, just not in the way we understand life.

61.quote: There will always be some moments in life when even you won't believe what you've done, yet there you are, having done it, either exceptionally or humorously.
